It is a recognizable Olympic contest; the exact English spelling is dec + athlon, so do not double-count the a when explaining the diachronic déca- + -athlon description. deca→decathlon e_7050183c81abdb9d8785 and dec→decathlon e_cc82172c8cf0cd10229e were previously accepted on their respective numeral-source scopes, and remain unchanged.

AHD and Oxford independently identify Greek pente five and athlon contest; Garner separately lists pentathlon as an instance of -athlon. The word was borrowed from Greek and is a historical model for later reanalysis, not a claim that an English suffix was used in its original Greek formation. The exact surface is pent + athlon; AHD's penta- + athlon description involves an overlapping/coalesced vowel rather than an extra a. It is familiar from sports coverage, though more domain-specific than triathlon. penta→pentathlon e_9707e235b060b2baaf3e and pent→pentathlon e_8e549d058b8c705a48ad accepted within their own numeral source scopes; no change to those decisions.

Garner explicitly labels -athlon a suffix, gives its Greek contest meaning, and cites triathlon, pentathlon and decathlon; an independent Nelson English primary school textbook explicitly identifies athlon as contest and explains triathlon. Etymonline gives tri- + Greek athlon, modelled on other event names, and MW verifies the familiar modern race. This word names a real sport encountered in everyday news and fitness; preserve Greek final element as a full combining form and note that -athon and -thon are separately reanalysed event suffixes, not the source of -athlon. The existing athl→triathlon word edge already exists, so the proposed new spelling is not a new example. Independent cross-check: Garner’s Modern English Usage explicitly calls -athlon a suffix from Greek contest and lists triathlon. Nelson English Pupil Book 6 independently identifies Greek athlon contest and describes triathlon as three-part swimming, cycling and running; indexed text was accessible though direct fetch hit tool content-size limit. Etymonline explicitly gives tri- plus Greek athlon formed on decathlon and biathlon, and Merriam-Webster confirms common sport. Distinguish -athon/-thon separately abstracted from marathon; no claim that these are false or that they generated the exact triathlon boundary.
